title: Numbers
description: Count things, and say how many there are.
grammarNote: Un and una mean one, and they match the noun: un libro, una casa.

explanation.summary: Numbers from one to a hundred are almost all regular, and the article un and una is the number one in front of a noun. Once you know uno, dieciséis, veintiún and cien, you can count anything.

sections.heading: The regular ones
sections.body: Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez. Then the pattern changes at sixteen: dieciséis, veintiuno, veintidós, and the tens are veinti, treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien. A number over fifteen is written as one word.

sections.heading: Un and una
sections.body: Un is masculine and una is feminine, and it is only used in front of a noun. On its own you say uno: uno, dos, tres. There is also un as a word meaning a, for something you have not mentioned: un amigo, a friend, someone.

sections.heading: When you count things
sections.body: After a number greater than one you use de before the noun: dos cafés, tres sillas. So you say dos cafés, not dos cafés de. With a person you count how many there are, and the number comes first: hay dos personas, there are two people. There is no plural form of the number itself.

examples.es: Hay dos sillas en la cocina.
examples.en: There are two chairs in the kitchen.

items.note: One. Before a noun it becomes un or una.
Cien is one hundred. For hundreds it is ciento.

drills.meaning: there are two chairs in the kitchen
drills.note: The number comes first and the noun follows directly.
After a number the noun takes de.
On its own you say uno, not un.
